715.title: The great persecution (303)
715.hook: Diocletian orders churches destroyed and scriptures burned
715.howItsDone: Catholics honor the martyrs of this persecution in the Church's calendar, and the Church still asks the faithful to pray for Christians who suffer for their faith today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agnes, too small for the chains. Your line was the lamb. Did a young person hear an encouraging word from you? Day seven hundred fifteen.

At first light, soldiers and officials force open the doors of a church. It stands in Nicomedia, the city where the emperor Diocletian keeps his court, and the emperors are watching from the palace. Inside, the officials search for an image of God and find none. They find the scriptures, and burn them. They take what they want. Then the guard is sent in with axes and tools, and in a few hours the building is flat. The writer Lactantius tells it this way. It's the opening scene of what Christians came to call the great persecution.
screen: `AT FIRST LIGHT.` → `THE EMPERORS WATCH.` → `THE SCRIPTURES BURN.`

segments.voice: First, the order. Lactantius says an edict came out the next day. Christians lost their rank and their protection under the law. Eusebius, the historian, says the imperial letters ordered churches torn down to their foundations and the scriptures destroyed by fire. Second, the fire in the square. Eusebius writes that he saw it with his own eyes: houses of prayer thrown down, and the holy scriptures burned in the middle of the marketplaces. Not a rumor. A thing he watched. Third, the people who said no. In a town in North Africa, the officials came to Bishop Felix and demanded the church's books. The account of his trial gives his answer, simply: I have them, but I won't give them up. He was put to death for it. Others hid the books, or handed over something else in their place. Fourth, the people who said yes. Some clergy did hand the books over to save their lives. Christians in North Africa called them traditores, those who handed over, and the arguments about whether they could still serve as priests and bishops ran on long after the danger was gone. It's an uncomfortable part of the story, and an honest one: courage and fear in the same churches. Tradition places Agnes, from yesterday, in this same storm.
screen: `THE EDICT.` · `BURNED IN THE MARKETPLACE.` · `I HAVE THEM. I WON'T GIVE THEM.` · `THOSE WHO HANDED THEM OVER.` · then, large: `THEY HID THE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those who hide their Bibles today. Settle, and breathe. If there's a Bible or a prayer book near you, put your hand on it, or just picture one on a shelf. Notice how ordinary it is to own it. Now think of people for whom it isn't ordinary: someone keeping a few pages hidden, reading at night, sharing a single copy with friends, afraid of a knock at the door. Stay with that picture for a while. If you pray, you can ask for a safe place for them to read. The bell holds the time.
The great persecution. The emperor's order to tear down churches and burn the scriptures, and the Christians who hid the books. Today's word.
Your line: they hid the books. Today, open a Bible, or a page of one online, and read a single verse slowly, as something someone once kept safe. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Constantine (312–313)
716.hook: the emperor's victory, the Edict of Milan, and a freedom that brought new temptations
716.howItsDone: In Catholic tellings of Church history, Constantine's reign marks the end of the great persecution and the start of the Church's public life in the empire, with new freedom and new temptations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great persecution, churches torn down and scriptures burned. Your line was they hid the books. Which verse did you read slowly? Day seven hundred sixteen.

Two Christian writers of the emperor's own time tell the same story, and they don't tell it the same way. Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the throne. Lactantius says he was told in a dream to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. Eusebius, writing later, says Constantine told him, and swore to it, that he saw a sign of light in the sky, a cross above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. Either way, he wins. And the world of the persecuted Church turns upside down.
screen: `TWO WRITERS, ONE STORY.` → `A SIGN ON THE SHIELDS.` → `BY THIS, CONQUER.`

segments.voice: First, the sign. It's honest to say the sources differ: a dream in one, a vision in the sky and then a dream in the other. What they agree on is that Constantine put a Christian sign on his army, and credited his victory to Christ. Second, the letter. Afterward, Constantine and his fellow emperor Licinius agree on a policy, and Lactantius copies the letter that announces it. It grants to Christians, and to all others, the free choice to follow whatever worship each person wants. Church buildings and property taken in the persecution are to be given back. People call it the Edict of Milan. Remember Nicomedia, and the books burning in the market square. Now Christians can ask for their churches back. Third, the surprise. Freedom was a gift, and it came with new temptations. The emperor gave the church money, buildings and favor. Bishops found themselves near the throne. Being Christian became useful for a career. Eusebius himself, who admired Constantine, complains in his Life of Constantine about hypocrites who slipped into the Church to win the emperor's goodwill. And Constantine, Eusebius says, was baptized only near the end of his life. Fourth, why it matters now. Persecution asks one question: will you stay? Comfort asks a quieter one: why are you here? The Church after Constantine had to learn to answer the second question.
screen: `TWO TELLINGS OF ONE SIGN.` · `FREEDOM FOR CHRISTIANS AND ALL OTHERS.` · `NEW TEMPTATIONS.` · `WHY ARE YOU HERE?` · then, large: `FREEDOM, AND ITS DANGERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what comfort does to faith. Settle, and breathe. Think back to a stretch of your life when things were hard, and then to a stretch when things were easy. In each one, where was your attention? On God, on the people you love, on what matters most to you? Don't judge it. Just notice what changed, if anything did. Then look at today. Is anything comfortable crowding out something that matters? If you pray, you can bring that to God honestly. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. The emperor who won under a Christian sign, granted freedom of worship, and brought the Church both peace and new temptations. Today's word.
Your line: freedom, and its dangers. Today, notice one comfort you lean on, and ask the quiet question: why am I here? Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: Helena in Jerusalem
717.hook: the emperor's mother builds churches at the holy places; tradition says she found the cross
717.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Helena as a saint, and pilgrims still travel to the churches at the holy places in Bethlehem and Jerusalem; parishes often take up collections for Christians in the Holy Land.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine: an emperor's victory, and a Church suddenly free to worship in the open. Your line was freedom, and its dangers. What did you notice comfort doing to faith? Day seven hundred seventeen.

The emperor's mother is packing for a long road east. Her name is Helena, and her son is Constantine. She has every reason to stay home. She could send architects. She could send gold and a letter with the imperial seal. Instead she goes herself, to the land where the Gospels happened. Bishop Eusebius, who wrote a life of her son, says she went to give thanks and to pray in the places where the Savior had walked. Not a tour of inspection. A pilgrimage.
screen: `THE EMPEROR'S MOTHER.` → `SHE COULD HAVE SENT GOLD.` → `SHE WENT HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Start with what Eusebius tells us. Helena dedicated two churches. One stood over the cave at Bethlehem where, Christians said, Jesus was born. The other stood on the Mount of Olives, at the place of the ascension. Bricks and columns, yes, but the point was simple: to mark the spots where God had come close, so pilgrims could stand there too. Second, the road itself. Eusebius says that as she traveled she gave freely: to whole towns, to soldiers, to people who had nothing to wear, to prisoners, some of whom she set free. And he says that in church she didn't sit apart in imperial splendor. She came in plain clothes and prayed among ordinary worshippers. Third, the story that travels with her name. Tradition says that in Jerusalem Helena searched for the cross of Christ, and found it. Here it helps to be honest about the sources. Eusebius, who describes her journey and her churches, says nothing about a cross. The story of the finding appears in later writers, among them Saint Ambrose of Milan. The Church honors relics of the cross, and the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross recalls them. Catholics and Orthodox Christians honor Helena as a saint, whatever a historian decides about the details. Fourth, why her trip still matters. In Luke's Gospel, after the angels leave, the shepherds say: "Let us go over to Bethlehem, and let us see this word that is come to pass." Eusebius says Helena made her journey in old age. Like the shepherds, she didn't settle for hearing about it. She went to see. And today Christians still live in Bethlehem and Jerusalem and Nazareth, and still pray in churches near the places she marked.
screen: `TWO CHURCHES SHE BUILT.` · `GIFTS ALONG THE ROAD.` · `TRADITION SAYS: THE CROSS.` · `LET US GO OVER TO BETHLEHEM.` · then, large: `SHE WENT TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people who live in those places now. Settle, and breathe. Bethlehem. Jerusalem. Nazareth. Towns with Christian families who worship near the old holy places, alongside neighbors of other faiths. Picture one street, one church door, one family getting ready for Sunday. If you pray, you can pray for Christians in the Holy Land, and for peace for everyone who lives there. If you don't, simply keep them in mind, one town at a time. The bell holds the time.
Helena in Jerusalem. The emperor's mother who traveled to the holy places, built churches, gave to the poor, and, tradition says, found the cross. Today's word.

Your line: she went to see. Today, go in person to one thing you've only heard about: a neighbor's garden, a friend's new place, a church down the road you've never walked into. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Anthony of the desert (c. 251–356)
718.hook: hearing the gospel of the rich young man, he sells everything and goes into the desert
718.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns live under vows in monasteries, praying together through the day, and the Church keeps the feast of Saint Anthony the Abbot each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Helena in Jerusalem, building churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. Your line was she went to see. Where did you go in person? Day seven hundred eighteen.

A young man in Egypt is walking to church, turning something over in his mind. His parents have died. He's been left land, and a younger sister to look after. On the way he's thinking about the apostles, who left everything to follow Jesus, and about the believers in Acts, who sold what they had and laid the money at the apostles' feet. He walks in just as the Gospel is being read. It's the story of the rich young man. His name is Anthony, and what he does next starts something.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN WITH LAND.` → `THINKING ABOUT THE APOSTLES.` → `THE GOSPEL IS BEING READ.`

segments.voice: Here is the line he heard, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor." In the Gospel, the rich young man hears it and goes away sad. Anthony's biographer, Saint Athanasius, says Anthony heard it as if it had been read for him alone. So he did the thing the young man in the Gospel couldn't. He gave his family's land to the people of his village. He sold the rest of what he owned and gave the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister. Then, the story goes, he walked into church another day and heard Jesus say not to be anxious about tomorrow. So he gave away the rest, and placed his sister with a community of women who had given their lives to God. Next, the desert. He didn't vanish all at once. Athanasius describes him first learning from an old man near his village, copying the good habits of people around him: one in prayer, another in kindness, another in fasting. Then he went farther out, to tombs, to an empty fort, and at last into the mountains, praying, working with his hands, and struggling, in Athanasius's telling, against temptations that came at him like enemies. And then the strange part. He went to be alone, and people followed him. They came for advice, for healing, for a word. Some stayed and built huts nearby. Athanasius says the desert became like a city, filled with monks. That's today's word. A monk is someone who leaves ordinary life to live for God in prayer, alone or with others. Catholic monks and nuns still do, in monasteries around the world. Tradition calls Anthony the father of monks. It began with one Gospel line, heard on an ordinary walk to church.
screen: `IF THOU WILT BE PERFECT.` · `HE GAVE IT AWAY.` · `FARTHER INTO THE DESERT.` · `THE DESERT FILLS WITH MONKS.` · then, large: `HE HEARD AND WENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away one thing. Nobody is asking you to sell the house. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk through your home: a closet, a shelf, a drawer. Find one thing you don't need that someone else could use. A coat. A book. A pan you have two of. Hold it in your mind and notice whether there is a small tug of wanting to keep it. If there is, that tug is where Anthony's story lives. If you pray, you can offer the thing, and the tug, to God. The bell holds the time.
Monk. Someone who leaves ordinary life to live for God in prayer, alone or with others. Tradition remembers Anthony of the desert as the father of monks. Today's word.
Your line: he heard and went. Today, take the thing you chose and give it to someone who can use it, before the day is out. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: Sit in your cell
719.hook: a desert father's advice: sit in your cell and your cell will teach you everything
719.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns keep times of silence in their cells and cloisters, and many lay Catholics set aside a quiet place at home for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anthony heard one Gospel line in church and walked into the desert. Your word was monk, and your line was he heard and went. What did you give away? Day seven hundred nineteen.

A brother has crossed the desert to Scetis to see an old monk called Abba Moses. He asks what visitors to the desert asked: give me a word. One saying to live by. Perhaps he expects something hard. Fasting. Vigils. A rule. The old man answers with one sentence. Go, sit in your cell, and your cell will teach you everything. And that's all. No program. No follow-up. A word that sounds too simple to work.
screen: `GIVE ME A WORD.` → `ONE SAYING TO LIVE BY.` → `GO, SIT IN YOUR CELL.`

segments.voice: Start with the title. The visitor calls him abba. It's the word for father, and Christians knew it from the Gospel: in Gethsemane, in Mark's telling, Jesus prays, "Abba, Father." In the desert, abba became the name for an elder whose life gave his words weight. People came to hear a few of them, and those short sayings were gathered into the collection we call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers. Next, the man. Tradition says Abba Moses had a rough past before he became a monk, and the sayings remember him for humility. Once, they say, the brothers called a meeting to judge a monk who had sinned. Moses at first refused to come. When they sent for him again, he came carrying a leaking jug of water. Asked why, he said his own sins were running out behind him where he couldn't see them, and here he was, coming to judge someone else's. The brothers said no more, and forgave the one who had sinned. Third, the cell. A monk's cell wasn't a prison. It was his small hut or room, the place he prayed, slept and worked. So why would a room teach everything? Some readers hear it this way: when you stop going elsewhere, you meet what you brought with you. Restlessness. Boredom. The itch to check on something, anything. The urge to leave. On that reading, those aren't distractions from the lesson. They are the lesson. Staying put, the sayings suggest, lets you see yourself without the usual escape routes, and that is where prayer starts to get honest. Fourth, your own cell. Your cell may not be a hut in Egypt. But there's a kitchen, a bedroom, a parked car, a desk at lunch. The advice travels. Stop moving for a while, and let the room do its teaching.
screen: `ABBA: FATHER.` · `THE LEAKING JUG.` · `A CELL IS A SMALL ROOM.` · `YOUR OWN CELL.` · then, large: `THE CELL TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay in one room. Wherever you are, that's your cell. Don't get up, don't tidy, don't reach for the phone. Settle, and breathe. Notice what wants to leave first: your hands, your eyes, your thoughts. Don't fight it. Just notice it, and stay. If you pray, you can say the two words from Gethsemane, Abba, Father, and let the rest be quiet. If you don't, let your breath be the only thing that moves. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Father: the word Jesus prays in Gethsemane, and the name the desert gave its elders. Today's word.
Your line: the cell teaches. Later today, sit in one room for five minutes with nothing to do, and see what it shows you. Day seven hundred nineteen.

720.title: The desert mothers
720.hook: Amma Syncletica and others taught that the real desert is the heart
720.howItsDone: Catholic women religious, including contemplative nuns, continue a life of prayer and silence, and the Church honors Saint Syncletica among the desert mothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abba Moses told a visitor to go and sit in his cell. Your word was abba, and your line was the cell teaches. What did the room show you? Day seven hundred twenty.

Turn the pages of the desert sayings and the title you keep meeting is abba. Abba this, abba that. Then, here and there, a different one. Amma Sarah. Amma Theodora. Amma Syncletica. Women who went out to pray in the wilderness too, and who were remembered not as someone's sister or someone's helper, but as teachers in their own right. People came to them asking for a word, just as they did with the men. And one of them moved the desert somewhere nobody expected.
screen: `ABBA, ABBA, ABBA.` → `THEN: AMMA.` → `TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN RIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Amma means mother. It carries the same weight as abba: not a family tie, but a spiritual one. An amma was an elder whose life had taught her something worth passing on, and whose few words people carried home. Second, one of them by name. Tradition says Syncletica came from a well-off family in Alexandria, gave away what she had, and lived a life of prayer and fasting near the city, not deep in the sand. Younger women gathered to learn from her, and a later writer collected her teaching into a life. Her sayings sit right beside the abbas' in the desert collection. Third, the turn. A desert mother might be expected to say: go to the desert. Syncletica says something sharper. Some who live out on the mountain, she warns, behave as if they were in town, and they're lost. And it's possible to live among a crowd and be solitary in your mind, while someone living alone can be living in a crowd of her own thoughts. Read that slowly. The quiet isn't guaranteed by the sand. The noise isn't guaranteed by the city. For Syncletica, the real desert, the place of prayer without distraction, is inside. Fourth, what that means on a Tuesday. A bus. A waiting room. A kitchen at dinnertime. The desert mothers didn't promise those places would go quiet. Syncletica's saying suggests the quiet can be found in them anyway, and that a person can carry a small wilderness through a loud day.
screen: `AMMA: MOTHER.` · `SYNCLETICA OF ALEXANDRIA.` · `A CROWD IN YOUR OWN THOUGHTS.` · `A DESERT YOU CAN CARRY.` · then, large: `THE DESERT IS WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the quiet inside, without needing the room to be quiet. Leave the noise around you as it is. Traffic, voices, a fridge humming: let them all stay. Settle, and breathe. Notice the crowd of your own thoughts, the way Syncletica describes it. Don't chase them out. Just step back from them, the way you'd step back from a busy street onto a doorstep. If you pray, you can rest in God's presence without saying anything at all. The bell holds the time.
Amma. Mother: the title the desert gave its women teachers, like Amma Syncletica. Today's word.
Your line: the desert is within. Today, in the loudest place you go, take three slow breaths and find the doorstep again. Day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: Pachomius
721.hook: a former soldier organizes monks into communities with shared work and prayer
721.howItsDone: Catholic monks and nuns who live in community share meals, work and the prayer of the hours under a rule and a superior, and the Church honors Saint Pachomius as a founder of that common life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert mothers, and Amma Syncletica's warning that a crowd can live inside your head. Your word was amma, and your line was the desert is within. Where did you find the doorstep? Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Down the Nile goes a boatload of new recruits, kept under guard at night, more like prisoners than soldiers. One of them is a young Egyptian, just drafted into the army. At one town, strangers come down to the boat with food and drink and look after them. He asks who these people are. Christians, he's told. They're kind to everyone, for the sake of God. That night, the story of his life says, he made a promise: if he got free, he would serve God and serve people. His name is Pachomius.
screen: `DRAFTED, UNDER GUARD.` → `STRANGERS BRING FOOD.` → `A PROMISE THAT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the kindness keeps working. Released from the army, Pachomius is baptized, and he goes to learn the desert life from an old hermit named Palamon. Hard teaching: little food, long prayer, manual work. He learns it. Second, the new thing. Anthony's way, which we met three days ago, was mostly the way of the hermit, alone or nearly. Pachomius gathers monks into a community. At a deserted village called Tabennesi, the story goes, he begins to build. One wall around them all. One rule. One table. The monks work, weaving mats and baskets, farming, cooking, nursing the sick, and what they make is for everyone. They pray together at set times. An abbot leads, and the brothers obey him, not as a general but as a father. Third, why it matters. The hermit's life suits a few. A shared life can hold many: the strong and the weak, the gifted and the ordinary. Some readers see in his communities the picture in Acts, where the believers held all things in common. Shared work can wear off rough edges in a way solitude may not, because the brother who annoys you is at breakfast tomorrow. Catholic religious orders that live in community stand in that line. Fourth, look back at this week. Under persecution, they hid the books. With Constantine came freedom, and its dangers. Helena went to see. Anthony heard and went. Abba Moses said the cell teaches. Syncletica said the desert is within. And today Pachomius says something the desert needed to hear: you don't have to go alone. Together in the desert.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one task with others. Settle, and breathe. Think through the work of your day: dishes, a report, a ride to school, a load of laundry, a meal. Which one do you usually do alone, a little resentfully, or a little proudly? Choose one, and picture doing it beside someone else instead. Not handing it off. Doing it together, the way Pachomius's monks wove and cooked side by side. Picture who it is. If you pray, you can ask a blessing on the work the two of you will share. The bell holds the time.
Pachomius. A former soldier, won over by strangers' kindness, who gathered monks into communities of shared work and prayer. Today's word.
Your line: together in the desert. Today, ask someone to do one ordinary task with you, and do it side by side. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

myth: Pachomius was a soldier before he was a monk
drafted as a young man; the kindness of Christians to the recruits turned him.
Pachomius's monks each lived alone and rarely met
they shared one wall, one rule, one table, work and prayer.
Pachomius taught himself the desert life
he first learned from an old hermit named Palamon.

fork.setup: you're a young recruit under guard on the Nile. strangers come with food and look after you. they're Christians. what do you do?
options: eat, and forget them.
promise to serve God and people if you get free.
slip away with them that night.
fork.reveal: his life says he made that promise, and kept it: baptism, the hermit Palamon, and then a whole community.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing — the word Acts uses for the believers' common life.

trapdoor: what you thought: monks always lived alone in caves.
what it means: Pachomius gathered them into communities with one rule, shared work, shared meals and prayer at set times.
what a scholar hears: koinonia, the fellowship of Acts, lived behind a wall at Tabennesi under an abbot.
